lessons.title: argc and argv
intro: A Unix program is started with a command line, like ./greet ken dennis. main can receive it: int main(int argc, char *argv[]). argc counts the words, and argv[0], argv[1], … are the words themselves.
argv[0] is the program's own name, so argc is always at least 1. atoi(argv[1]) turns a word like "42" into a number.
In this app, a comment like /* $ ./greet ken dennis */ at the top says how the program is started.

exercises.prompt: For ./copy a.txt b.txt, what is argc?

options: The first argument after the name
exercises.explanation: That's how a program can print its own name in error messages.
atoi turns each word into a number: 2 + 3 + 4.

exercises.prompt: Turn the first argument into a number.
This program crashes when it's started without arguments. Which line needs a check before it?
exercises.explanation: With no arguments, argc is 1 and argv[1] is NULL. Check if (argc < 2) first and print how to use the program.
One char * per word of the command line.

lessons.title: One Job, Done Well
intro: The Unix philosophy, in Doug McIlroy's words: write programs that do one thing and do it well, and that work together.
Many Unix tools are filters: they read stdin, change something, and write to stdout. They don't care where the text comes from or where it goes.
Here's a tiny filter that turns everything into capitals, with toupper from ctype.h.

exercises.prompt: What is a filter in Unix?
options: A program that reads stdin and writes changed text to stdout
exercises.explanation: sort, grep, tr and wc are all filters.

options: Small programs that do one thing well and work together
One big program that does everything
exercises.explanation: Combine small tools instead of writing a giant one.

exercises.prompt: Copy stdin to stdout, character by character.
exercises.explanation: getchar returns EOF at the end of the input.

exercises.prompt: Why is c an int and not a char in these loops?
options: EOF (-1) must be different from every real character
exercises.explanation: An int can hold all 256 characters plus EOF.
Characters that aren't lowercase letters stay as they are.
Every character except ' ' is passed through.

lessons.title: Pipes
intro: In 1973, Ken Thompson added pipes to Unix in one night: the | sign sends one program's stdout into the next one's stdin. who | wc -l counts the users logged in.
Because filters only use stdin and stdout, any of them can be plugged together, like pipes in a building. Your program can be part of a pipeline without knowing it.
A small grep: print only the lines that contain a word, using strstr from string.h, which finds a string inside another.

exercises.prompt: What does the | sign do in the Unix shell?
options: Sends one program's output into the next one's input

exercises.prompt: Why can any filter be used in a pipeline?
options: They only read stdin and write stdout
They are all written in C
exercises.explanation: The shell connects stdin and stdout; the program doesn't need to know.

exercises.prompt: What does strstr(line, "un") return when line doesn't contain "un"?
exercises.explanation: Otherwise it returns a pointer to where the match starts.

exercises.prompt: Print the line only if it contains the word.
exercises.explanation: strstr searches; strcmp only compares whole strings.

options: Ken Thompson, after Doug McIlroy pushed for them
exercises.explanation: McIlroy had wanted to connect programs "like garden hoses" for years.

options: stderr, so it isn't mixed into the pipeline's output
exercises.explanation: Errors should stay visible even in a pipeline.
